# Vectorization and connectivity {#lagoa-connectivity}

## Fragments as polygons {-}

To analyse connectivity, fragments need to become polygons.
`reclass_to_polygons()` performs that conversion from the reclassified maps and
keeps area, year and class identity. Here, the 2024 forest:

```{r}
polygons <- reclass_to_polygons(metrics, years = 2024, save_shp = FALSE)
```

There are `r nrow(polygons)` fragments, totalling `r num(sum(polygons$area_ha), 0)` ha.
With `save_shp = TRUE`, each year is also written as a shapefile.

## Connectivity at several thresholds {-}

`land_connectivity()` links fragments that lie closer than a maximum distance,
that is, the distance an organism can travel outside the forest, and computes
connectivity indices for each threshold:

```{r connectivity, fig.height=6}
connectivity <- land_connectivity(polygons, max_dist = c(100, 300, 600),
                                  language = "en")
connectivity$plot
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
cm <- connectivity$metrics
tabela(data.frame(`Maximum distance (m)` = cm$max_dist_m, Components = cm$graph_components,
                  `Isolated fragments` = cm$isolates, `IIC (×10⁻³)` = 1000 * cm$IIC, check.names = FALSE), 2)
```

For a species that only crosses 100 m of open land, the forest splits into
`r cm$graph_components[1]` disconnected groups, with `r cm$isolates[1]` isolated
fragments. At 300 m, `r cm$graph_components[2]` groups remain, and the integral
index of connectivity (IIC) becomes `r num(cm$IIC[2] / cm$IIC[1], 0)` times
larger. From 300 to 600 m, the gain is small: for species able to cross about
300 m, the remaining forest already works as a network.

## Priority fragments {-}

`patch_imp_fast()` measures how much connectivity would drop if each fragment
were removed, in the chosen scenario:

```{r}
scenario_300 <- connectivity$scenarios[["300"]]$land
importance <- patch_imp_fast(scenario_300, metric = "IIC")
```

```{r include=FALSE}
p <- sort(importance$prioritization, decreasing = TRUE)
```

Losing either of the two most important fragments would cut the IIC by
`r num(p[1], 1)`% and `r num(p[2], 1)`%, respectively, while `r sum(p < 5)` of
the `r length(p)` fragments reduce it by less than 5% each. The forest's
connectivity therefore depends on conserving a handful of fragments.

`land_connectivity()` already computes this prioritization for each threshold,
and the map shows how much the index would drop without each fragment:

```{r importance, fig.height=6}
connectivity$importance_plot
```

The IIC follows the definition of Pascual-Hortal and Saura (2006): isolated
fragments also count, through their own area. The `lconnect` value, which omits
them, is kept in `connectivity$metrics$IIC_lconnect`.

## Stepping stones and importance fractions {-}

Each fragment's importance splits into three parts (Saura and Rubio, 2010): the
fragment's own area (intra), its direct links to the others (flux), and its role
as a **stepping stone**, when it lies on the best path between two others
(connector). The probability of connectivity (PC; Saura and Pascual-Hortal,
2007) accounts for indirect paths and is the most suitable metric to identify
stepping stones. Here, with a 5% dispersal probability at 300 m:

```{r}
pc <- patch_imp_fast(scenario_300, metric = "PC", p_ref = 0.05, d_ref = 300)
head(pc$fractions)
```

```{r include=FALSE}
f <- pc$fractions
stepping <- sum(f$connector > 0.5 * pc$prioritization)
```

In `r stepping` fragments, more than half of the importance comes from the
connector role: small patches that matter more for their position than for their
area. In `land_connectivity()`, the fractions are stored in `patch_metrics`
(columns `dPC_intra`, `dPC_flux` and `dPC_connector`) and in `fraction_metrics`,
with the `fractions_plot` and `connector_plot` charts:

```{r fractions, fig.height=6}
connectivity_pc <- land_connectivity(polygons, max_dist = 300,
  metric_patch = c("IIC", "PC"), p_ref = 0.05, d_ref = 300, language = "en")
connectivity_pc$fractions_plot
```

PC is the most demanding index. In landscapes with hundreds of fragments,
`parallel = 4` (or another number of processes) splits the work across cores and
gives the same result; with a few dozen fragments, starting the processes costs
more than it saves. Exact pruning of PC links (`prune = "auto"`) is applied on its
own from 50 fragments upwards.

## Resistance and least-cost distance {-}

Straight-line distance treats the whole matrix as equal. A pasture, a sugarcane
field and a highway, however, do not pose the same difficulty to an organism
moving between fragments. `resistance_surface()` turns one year's land-use map
into a cost surface: each class gets a cost per metre travelled (1 equals
Euclidean distance), and `Inf` makes the class a barrier. The values below are
only illustrative; in practice they come from the literature or from experts on
the species of interest:

```{r resistance, fig.height=5}
costs <- c("3" = 1, "4" = 1, "11" = 2, "12" = 3, "9" = 5, "21" = 8, "15" = 10,
           "20" = 20, "39" = 20, "41" = 20, "25" = 50, "24" = 100, "33" = Inf)
resistance <- resistance_surface(maps, year = 2024, resistance = costs, default = 20,
                                 language = "en")
resistance$plot
```

Highways, dams and other barriers can be added as `sf` lines or polygons in
`barriers`, with their own cost or as impassable. `cost_distance()` then measures
the least accumulated cost from edge to edge between fragments, and the matrix
goes into `land_connectivity()` in place of Euclidean distance. Thresholds are
then given in cost units:

```{r cost}
cost <- cost_distance(polygons, resistance)
connectivity_cost <- land_connectivity(polygons, max_dist = 1500, distance = cost,
  metric_patch = c("IIC", "PC"), build_plot = FALSE)
```

Distance matrices from other sources are also accepted, such as the `From`, `To`
and `Distance` tables of `Makurhini::distancefile()`.

## Equivalent connected area and landscape fractions {-}

The equivalent connected area (ECA; Saura et al., 2011) expresses IIC and PC in
hectares: the area of a single fragment that would give the same connectivity.
In `metrics`, `ECA_IIC` and `ECA_PC` are in m², and `ECAnorm_IIC` and
`ECAnorm_PC` give it as a percentage of habitat. The `PC_intra`, `PC_direct` and
`PC_step` columns split the index, as in Makurhini, into the area of the
fragments themselves, direct links and the gain through stepping stones. `Prot`,
`ProtConn`, `ProtUnconn` and `RelConn` follow ProtConn (Saura et al., 2017), with
the forest taken as the protected area:

```{r echo=FALSE}
m <- connectivity_pc$metrics
tabela(data.frame(`ECA (ha)` = m$ECA_PC / 1e4, `ECA (% of habitat)` = m$ECAnorm_PC,
                  `Intra (%)` = m$PC_intra, `Direct (%)` = m$PC_direct,
                  `Stepping stones (%)` = m$PC_step, ProtConn = m$ProtConn, check.names = FALSE), 1)
```

## Links that hold the network together {-}

With `link_importance = TRUE`, each link gets the drop of the index when it alone
is removed. Links with an alternative path of equal cost are worth zero; the
highest values mark the irreplaceable links of the network:

```{r links, fig.height=6}
connectivity_links <- land_connectivity(polygons, max_dist = 300,
  metric_patch = c("IIC", "PC"), p_ref = 0.05, d_ref = 300, link_importance = TRUE,
  language = "en")
connectivity_links$link_plot
```

## Connectivity over time {-}

`connectivity_change()` repeats the analysis over several years and compares the
loss of habitat (dA) with the loss of connected area (dECA), like Makurhini's
`MK_dECA()`. When dECA falls more than dA, connectivity is being lost faster than
habitat:

```{r change, fig.height=5}
polygon_series <- reclass_to_polygons(metrics, years = c(1985, 2004, 2024), save_shp = FALSE)
change <- connectivity_change(polygon_series, max_dist = 300, metric_patch = c("IIC", "PC"),
  p_ref = 0.05, d_ref = 300, language = "en")
change$change_plot
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
s <- change$series[change$series$metric == "PC", ]
tabela(data.frame(Year = s$year, `Habitat (ha)` = s$habitat_ha, `ECA (ha)` = s$ECA_ha,
                  `dA (%)` = s$dA, `dECA (%)` = s$dECA, rECA = s$rECA, Change = s$change,
                  check.names = FALSE), 2)
```

`fractions_plot` shows how intra, direct links and stepping stones change over
the years, and `map_plot` the importance of fragments in each year. With
`animate = TRUE` and the gganimate package, `animation` shows the same map year
by year:

```{r eval=FALSE}
change <- connectivity_change(polygon_series, max_dist = 300, metric_patch = "PC",
  link_importance = TRUE, animate = TRUE, language = "en")
gganimate::animate(change$animation, fps = 1)
```

## Edge effects and an extended context {-}

The study-area boundary cuts fragments and hides the stepping stones outside
it, which underestimates connectivity near the edge. With `focal`,
`land_connectivity()` measures the connectivity of the study area's habitat
using its surroundings as stepping stones, and `connectivity_context()` does so
for several context radii: it extends the area, reloads the maps from the same
source, reclassifies and vectorizes once and reuses the distances of the largest
context for the smaller ones. Only the habitat classes are needed. Radius 0 is
the analysis without context:

```{r eval=FALSE}
context <- connectivity_context(maps, classes = 3, max_dist = 300,
  context = c(0, 300, 600, 1200, 2400), metric_patch = c("IIC", "PC"),
  p_ref = 0.05, d_ref = 300, language = "en")
context$sensitivity_plot
context$rank_stability
context$stepping_stones
```

When the ECA curve levels off (`converged`), the context no longer changes the
result; if it still grows at the largest radius, the edge effect persists and
the context should be widened. `rank_stability` shows whether the order of
priority fragments depends on the clip, and `stepping_stones` lists fragments
outside the area that sustain its connectivity. For a single context, without
the sensitivity analysis, use `load_rasters(context_m = 1000)`: the polygons
inherit the focal area and `land_connectivity()` uses it on its own.

With `targets`, the same analysis measures the importance of a fragment or of a
set of fragments removed at once, radius by radius. Comparing it with the sum
of single importances shows whether the fragments substitute for each other or
share the same contribution. Targets can be `fragment_id`, named lists of ids or
`sf` geometries, including outside the study area:

```{r eval=FALSE}
target <- connectivity_context(maps, classes = 3, max_dist = 300,
  targets = list(core = c(12, 40), corridor = 7), language = "en")
target$target_sensitivity
target$target_plot
```

The routine does not depend on MapBiomas: with `load_lulc()` (ESA WorldCover) it
works in any country, and `source` accepts a function that loads maps from
another source for the extended area.

## Integration with Makurhini {-}

`as_makurhini()` prepares the arguments of `MK_dPCIIC()`, `MK_dECA()` and
`MK_ProtConn()` with the same fragments, areas, boundary, distances and k
calibration, and with `run = TRUE` runs Makurhini when it is installed:

```{r eval=FALSE}
mk <- as_makurhini(connectivity_pc, "dPCIIC", run = TRUE)
protconn <- as_makurhini(connectivity_pc, "ProtConn", protected = protected_areas,
                         run = TRUE)
deca <- as_makurhini(change, "dECA", run = TRUE)
```
